item.title: Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang
item.abstract: Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV , a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7% . Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang . AKV is a Tsinghua serving system that lets LLM agents drop and reposition their own KV cache. Context engineering trims or summarizes the text history. Editing that prefix invalidates every later KV state. The retained suffix must then be re-prefilled. Harnesses therefore summarize late and aggressively, which can lose details from middle rounds. Cache engineering leaves the text trajectory untouched. It only changes which KV entries stay visible to attention. Retained entries are reused without recomputation. They can still carry information from dropped messages. In the research paper’s cost analysis, KV cache reads made up 82.4% of total API cost. AKV defines 3 cache operations. Append is the standard update for new tokens. Drop removes selected entries from future attention without changing positions. Repos rewrites retained keys to positions 0 through r-1 using a RoPE rotation . Values stay unchanged, so no hidden states are recomputed. In ablations, adding Repos raised GPT-OSS-120B’s BrowseComp-Plus pass rate from 55% to 62%. The hard part is serving. Identical tokens can produce different cache states under different operation histories. Plain prefix matching could reuse the wrong states. AKV extends SGLang’s radix tree with drop and reposition nodes. It frees dropped KV only when no active request still needs it. Segment-batch attention restores evicted states in 1 prefill pass. The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible . Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. drop_message maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. reposition lists the indices after which positions get compacted. A CachePolicy builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A CacheTool lets the model call drop_context itself. The main policy is a tool-response rolling drop that keeps the latest 12 tool responses. The Standard baseline summarizes at 96K tokens (192K for MiroThinker). Text Engineering summarizes at 48K. Benchmarks are BrowseComp-Plus , GAIA-Text , SWE-bench Verified and xbench-DeepSearch-2510 . Average pass rate (%) and cost (US cents per task) across 4 benchmarks. Source: Table 1 of the paper . AKV also cuts cost 21.9% versus Text Engineering. The accuracy gap opens on long runs. On BrowseComp-Plus at 96K tokens and above, GPT-OSS-120B scores 37% with AKV. Standard scores 24% and Text Engineering 32%, per the project page . Costs are API-equivalent estimates from published rates. Repositioned tokens are charged at the cache-hit rate, a deliberately conservative choice. Serving tests ran GPT-OSS-120B on 80 long-context SWE-bench Verified tasks. At each method’s peak setting, AKV delivers 1.18x output throughput and 1.53x input throughput. P95 request latency is 1.51x faster. At concurrency 16, Standard’s P95 latency hits 229.90 seconds versus 30.63 for AKV. KV pressure pushes Standard into repeated re-prefill. Per decode step, full-attention time falls from 7.082 to 2.849 ms. On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a GPU budget, AKV reached about 47% pass rate. Standard reached 40.7% and Text Engineering 32.3%. MiniMax-M2.7 refined policies on 20 BrowseComp-Plus tasks, then ran 100 held-out tasks. The iteration-6 policy cut cost 17.8% versus Standard at baseline accuracy. The abstract reports 7.1% savings beyond the expert-designed policy. Exposing cache control as a tool also helped accuracy. GPT-OSS-120B rose from 52.1 to 61.0 on a 100-task subset. MiniMax-M2.7’s cost rose, though, from 5.4 to 5.9 cents. The main numbers come from each project’s own paper and use different setups. They are not directly comparable. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and Project Page . item.title: Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls
item.abstract: Nace AI has released Drex for Search , which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question. Nace AI frames search as a series of decisions. Drex for Search applies its Drex models to those decisions. Drex scores given options with a calibrated probability each, in 1 forward pass. That makes it cheap enough for every agent step. The release targets classic RAG, which Nace sums up as chunk, embed, top-k, hope. The pipeline breaks in 3 cases: Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand. Nace AI tested 9 agent and model pairs on OfficeQA Pro , a 133-question benchmark over U.S. Treasury Bulletins. Key highlights: 6% more answers right, 62% fewer steps, 56% fewer tokens, and 2.3x faster. BrowseComp-Plus asks a deep-research agent 830 multi-hop questions over about 100K fixed web documents. With GPT-5, Nace AI reports: On VisDocAgentBench , an agent finds 1 target page among 2,375 arXiv pages. Drex for Search scores 77.5% R@1 with an open-weight Qwen 27B planner. The best published agent, Claude Opus 5, scores 67.5%. R@1 is 97.5% on direct questions, 77.5% on one bridge, and 57.5% on two. On MADQA , agents answer over 800 PDFs and cite pages. Nace reports 94.7% accuracy with Gemini 3.5 Flash and a page-attribution F1 of 88.2. Its effort calibration (Kuiper) is 6.66. Nace ranks it #1, based on the leaderboard as read on October 20. With open-weight Qwen 27B, Nace reports 93.4%. On EnterpriseRAG-Bench , with 500,000+ internal company documents, Nace reports an overall score of 88.22, which it ranks #3. That is 27.2 points above OpenAI File Search (61.03). Ranks and scores are as published by Nace AI , from leaderboards read October 20, 2026. Drex for Search runs in the Nace API Console , with 4 ways in on one key: Check out the Drex for Search page , API Console , Docs and Hugging Face . Thanks to the Nace AI team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by Nace AI. item.title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
item.abstract:
This is a melanoma. Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view. It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer. The test # The lesions come from MILK10k , a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology: 100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses. 100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses. Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician. Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly. Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma. Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it. Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case. The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses. You can try the CNN yourself . Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions. item.title: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM
item.abstract:
When I use an open-weight model, I see results that are nowhere close to what the quality benchmarks indicate. Tool call accuracy is an important part of serving open-weight models. When your tool calls aren’t accurate, the model builds up on nonsensical context. This leads to low quality results, particularly for agentic workloads where multi-turn sessions are common. Sadly, many providers and widely-used inference engines don’t fully pass tool-call accuracy tests . For example, when we served Kimi K2.6 with vLLM version 0.28, we got the expected tool call schema only 92% of the time. In other words, 2 out of every 25 attempted tool calls failed. Fortunately, vLLM recently added support for constrained decoding , a technique to guarantee schema-adherence. This feature has then been released as a server-side flag in vLLM 0.31. By enabling it, you can get to 100% schema accuracy with the newer Kimi and DeepSeek models. In this blog post, we first describe tool call schema accuracy and why it’s important in serving agentic workloads. We then talk about constrained decoding and how it fixes the schema accuracy problem. You can enable an LLM to call an external tool in two steps: (1) inform the AI model about the existence of externally available tool calls and (2) provide the model with instructions on how to output structured tool-calls. For example, when connecting OpenCode to Kimi, OpenCode sends Kimi a JSON array describing available tools. One of the tools in this list is webfetch , which fetches Web page contents: The inference engine then wraps this JSON description in LLM-specific tokens before passing it into the LLM, to match how the LLM was trained to recognize tool declarations. When serving Kimi, this looks something like: The JSON object describing the tool (or function , in the JSON above) includes the tool’s parameters, their types, which of the parameters are required, etc. This is known as the tool’s schema . For an agent harness (e.g., OpenCode) to successfully execute a tool call generated by the LLM, the call must follow the rules specified in its schema. Then, when a user asks to fetch a Web page via their agent harness, the LLM may output the following tokens: These tokens are parsed by the inference server’s parser, extracting the LLM-specific tokens and turning the call into a JSON object such as: This is then sent back to your harness (OpenCode, in our example), which runs its webfetch tool and sends its output back to the model. For a tool-call to succeed, the call must adhere to the tool’s schema. The simple approach to tool calling is to let the model generate tool calls freely and trust that the model’s training is sufficient to generate correct calls. This is similar to how we trust the model to generate syntactically correct prose. The simple approach works most of the time because modern models are good at following structured patterns. But success “most of the time” implies that many tool calls can still fail, resulting in context window pollution due to error messages, lower model performance, and increased cost due to the agent having to retry the call one or more times. To avoid such experiences when using Kimi, Moonshot AI published their K2VV ToolCall benchmark. This benchmark lets providers verify that they serve Kimi with the same quality as the original, including its default behavior of only generating valid tool calls. K2VV ToolCall’s workload consists of 2000 requests selected to evaluate when the LLM generates tool calls and whether the generated tool calls are syntactically correct (i.e., adhere to the provided schema). The benchmark allows analyzing the model’s quality by quantifying two metrics: trigger similarity and schema accuracy . Trigger similarity considers when the service decides to trigger a tool call, and how similar its decisions are to Moonshot AI’s own service. Schema accuracy quantifies the fraction of tool-calls that adhere to the tool’s schema and can therefore be invoked successfully. For example, when tool-call accuracy is 50%, half of the tool calls generated by the model are malformed. Schema accuracy usually falls short due to the probabilistic nature of language models. A model generates tokens based on likelihood. It is not running a compiler or type checker. Even with a clear prompt, it can still produce malformed tool calls. This can be caused by, for example, a mismatch between the model’s training data and the current inference harness. Models are trained on many tool-calling datasets, each with its own tools, schemas, and conventions. As a result, a model may generate a tool or field name that it has seen during the training, even if it does not exist in the current production environment. For example, it may generate search_web when the available tool is web_search , or use city_name when the active schema expects location . An LLM computes for each token the probability that it is the next in the sequence. It then selects the next token by performing a weighted sample. Constrained decoding avoids malformed tool calls by preventing models from sampling tokens that would result in a syntactically invalid tool call. When using constrained decoding, instead of letting the model sampling tokens freely and validating the result afterward, the inference engine guides generation step by step. At each step, only valid tokens are allowed. Which tokens are allowed is determined by the provided tool schema. vLLM implements this using structural tags from the XGrammar library . The snippet below shows an excerpt of how XGrammar implements constrained decoding in Kimi K2.6. It defines the valid structure of a tool call, including where the call begins, where the index appears, where the arguments begin, and where schema-constrained JSON must be generated. You can find the full implementation here . With this definition, generation must follow a valid path: Begin tool call → Tool name → Tool call index → Begin arguments → Schema-constrained JSON → End tool call Invalid paths are blocked during generation. For example, when generation reaches the tool-call index phase, the engine restricts sampling to integer tokens and masks out everything else. The figure below, reproduced from XGrammar’s article, provides a good visualization of how invalid tokens are masked. Source: Dong, Yixin, et al. "XGrammar: Flexible and efficient structured generation engine for large language models." Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 7 (2025). [ link ] This changes schema accuracy from a best-effort approach to a runtime guarantee. The model still decides which token to generate, but now the token is selected from a restricted and syntactically-correct set. Notably, this runtime enforcement adds negligible performance overhead. By precomputing token masks for each phase, and applying them efficiently on the GPU during generation, XGrammar guarantees correct tool calls without trading off significant performance. Moonshot AI recommends constrained decoding to be turned on and its own API behaves as such. So we initially added constrained decoding in our fork of vLLM. After vLLM added this feature in v0.25, we switched to using this feature from upstream for Kimi and DeepSeek. Unfortunately not long after, we found out that our tool-call accuracy score dropped back to 91%! After analyzing the problem, we confirmed that vLLM’s implementation of constrained decoding was still correct. Instead, we found that vLLM changed its default behavior for requests that do not explicitly turn constrained decoding on. This is primarily because vLLM is designed to support a wide range of models. Supporting constrained decoding is a per-model task and problems fall into three camps: Due to these issues, vLLM maintainers reported seeing problems with several models after constrained decoding was enabled.

item.title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again. In the movie Groundhog Day , Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years. Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again. Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price. In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent. Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains: What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching: Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill . During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token. Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint . You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so. Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both? For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically. New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents. The first win is to cache the static part of the prompt: the tools and instructions that stay the same across requests. These examples use your existing Amazon Bedrock client, TOOLS , and task . Replace the shortened INSTRUCTIONS string with your real policies and examples. The reusable prefix must reach 1,024 tokens to qualify. When caching static content, use explicit mode: choose where the saved prefix ends. The prompt_cache_key tells the service which requests are meant to share a cache. We come back to how to use it when we get to reading the cache in new sessions. In one of our tests using explicit caching, the roughly 4,000-token tools-and-instructions prefix wrote 4,120 tokens on the first request and read those 4,120 tokens on later requests. The task (or user request) comes after the cache boundary, so this doesn’t trigger a write to the cache. Keep in mind that prompt caching works only when you pass exactly the same text. Make sure that the agent’s instructions and tool lists are serialized the same way every time. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and other forms of tool delivery need to be indexed to make sure they stay consistent. Keep anything that varies, such as the date, the user’s name, or a request ID, after the cached instructions. As the content grows and varies (different tools and content), use implicit mode to let the service follow the conversation. Here, the first request has no explicit marker. Its latest eligible message is the user’s task, so the automatic breakpoint comes after that task and covers the tools, instructions, and task together. The mode is shown explicitly in the following example for clarity, even though implicit is the default. Setting store=False leaves conversation history in your application. It doesn’t disable caching. This is useful when the next turn continues the same task. A different task doesn’t match the prefix through the old task, and the implicit write doesn’t necessarily create a separate entry for only the tools and instructions. Use an explicit marker there when you need that shorter shared prefix to be reusable across tasks. Use both when the agent needs a shared starting point and a growing history. Start with the marked developer block in the following code example and call the function ask_with_implicit_cache . The request-level mode stays implicit. The block-level marker adds an explicit save point after the instructions. The service can also save through the latest eligible message. This keeps the shared prefix available while the conversation grows. The model requests tools by name and supplies their arguments. Your application must execute them. execute_function is a helper you build to route those requests to the matching Python functions and return their results. The following loop uses this helper to run each requested tool. It appends the model’s output and all tool results to the history list, then sends that list again until the model returns a final answer. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can reuse the unchanged prefix and cache the added content through the last tool result. Keep earlier messages and the initial TOOLS unchanged. For follow-ups, append a new user message and call the helper again. Keep earlier messages unchanged so their cached endpoints remain available. Rolling breakpoints: Each turn reads everything before it Figure 3: Rolling breakpoints, where each turn reads everything before it and writes only its own tool result For a separate explicit-only run, recreate the two-message history from the combined Hello cached world example. We decouple the problem into an identity stage that builds a representation of the subject’s geometry and appearance offline, and an animation stage that predicts expression-dependent residuals on top of it at runtime. This separation offers a favorable trade-off with respect to fidelity, quality and runtime: the identity stage can be expensive while the animation stage runs a lightweight network, optimized for mobile devices. Our method performs animation in a semantically structured latent space of a pretrained reconstruction model, where expression changes remain spatially contained, making residual prediction efficient. This reconstruction prior provides a consistent spatial layout, allowing fusion of multiple input views into a compact, fixed-size canonical Gaussian representation. While this two-stage design improves the runtime-quality trade-off, it still inherits a problem common to all expression-driven avatar methods: expression codes describe only the face and thus omit body pose and clothing position, making these regions underspecified in the input. The animation network faces an ill-posed mapping and resorts to averaging over conflicting body appearances, producing blur and temporal flicker. We address this with a body alignment network that learns to align the person’s body in the target image with the input reference images, removing the ambiguity from the training signal. item.title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
item.abstract: This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated. It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question , and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen. Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works. In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published. This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order. If you read the 2024 post , the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. If you didn’t, this post stands on its own. The services at play and the path one question takes through them: the agent decides whether to retrieve and which knowledge base to consult, the Gateway exposes each knowledge base as a tool it can call, the Managed Knowledge Bases search and cite, and the loop repeats as many times as the question needs. Everything the agent does along the way lands in Amazon CloudWatch. Figure 1: The services involved and the path a single question takes through them Before the walkthrough, it helps to establish three things: what makes retrieval agentic, why the Managed Knowledge Base is the right foundation for it, and why observability and evaluation belong in the design rather than bolted on later. Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start. Amazon Bedrock now offers a Managed Knowledge Base (Type: MANAGED): Amazon Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you, including embedding and reranking with service-managed models by default, so there is no vector database to provision, scale, or patch . This differs from a Customer-managed (DIY) Knowledge Base, where you choose and operate the vector store (for example, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) yourself. Two differences matter most for this solution: Because agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector are available only on the managed knowledge base, it is the natural foundation for enterprise agentic retrieval. It also means Amazon Bedrock manages the storage and indexing for you, so there is no OpenSearch Serverless collection or OCU capacity to provision in this design. The customer-managed option remains the right choice when you want to select and operate your own vector store, for example to reuse an existing OpenSearch Serverless collection or to meet specific data-residency, tuning, or compliance requirements. For enterprise agentic retrieval, the managed knowledge base is what makes the capability possible. An agentic system that returns an answer isn’t enough for production. You need to see how it behaves (latency, call volume, token usage), how good the retrieval and answers are, and you need those signals continuously. This solution ships two CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation (on-demand and continuous), all provisioned by the same CDK application. The grounding, citations, and evaluation layers also support responsible use. Cited answers trace back to their source passages so responses stay auditable, and the faithfulness and correctness scores let you catch answers drifting from their sources rather than finding out in production. Any infrastructure-as-code tool can create these resources. CDK earns its place here for a reason specific to this architecture: the four stacks are densely cross-referenced . The Gateway needs both knowledge base ids. The agent needs the URL and ARN for the Gateway. The dashboards need the KB ids, the Gateway ARN, and the agent runtime id, seven values crossing stack boundaries, each one a dimension on a metric or a target on a connector. Written as raw templates, that is a set of stack exports and cross-stack lookups kept in agreement by hand, plus a script that deploys in the right order and threads outputs forward, and both drift the moment anything is renamed. In CDK you pass the construct, and the export and the dependency edge are derived from that one act of passing it. The 2024 solution had three stacks and a mostly linear dependency chain. At four stacks with seven values crossing between them, the difference stops being stylistic. Here is the path a single question takes through the system, end to end. It’s worth a slow look, because the rest of the post walks through it left to right. The following diagram traces the end-to-end agentic retrieval workflow. A user’s question enters the agent on the AgentCore Runtime, which routes it through the AgentCore Gateway to one of two AgenticRetrieveStream tools, one per managed knowledge base, financial and weather, each ingested from Amazon S3.

item.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
item.abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection”. In a related attack, an agent “alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal”. During this attack the agent’s chain of thought read as: “Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.” Why this matters – fighting agents is very difficult : AI systems are increasingly creative, very fast, and have the ability to stay focused on a task and keep trying things. Fighting AI systems is akin to ensuring no leaks in a pipe with water flowing through it; at some point if you increase the pressure of the water (e.g., the intelligence and volume of the AI system), then the water will burst through the pipe. Read more : Securing our frontier model training environment (OpenAI blog) . What RSI looks like – one person pretrains a decent model from scratch: …Mirendil reveals what AI R&D optimization can do… In a sign of how massively augmented AI research is getting, a single researcher at AI R&D startup Mirendil has trained a decent coding model by themselves. The announcement of Mirendil-Base is the first major output from the startup and is less a technical breakthrough and more a proof-of-concept for how AI development could work in the future – a single human working in partnership with AI can build systems that would have taken teams of ten or more people to do a year ago. What they did: Mirendill-Base is a pretrained LLM “built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10m in compute,” Mirendil writes. “This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.” All the code was written from scratch on top of libraries like PyTorch and JAX, and the model learned only from publicly available data.

item.title: Nanbeige Releases Nanbeige4.3-33B, a 33B Open Agentic Coding Model
item.abstract: Nanbeige LLM Lab has released Nanbeige4.3-33B on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Nanbeige4.3-33B is a 33B dense language model built for agentic coding and office-style ‘cowork’ tasks. The lab sits inside the recruitment platform BOSS Zhipin . It also published Nanbeige4.3-33B-Base for custom post-training. The model supports a 524,288-token context window. In the lab’s own table, it leads 17 of 20 benchmarks against 3 open models near 30B. Nanbeige4.3-33B is the flagship ‘teacher’ model of the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab’s stated strategy is to build a strong teacher first. It then plans to distill agentic skills into smaller models, starting with Nanbeige4.3-3B. The config.json declares a standard LlamaForCausalLM architecture. There is no expert routing, so all 33B parameters run on every token. The chat template exposes 3 controls. enable_thinking toggles reasoning and is on by default. preserve_thinking keeps reasoning from earlier turns. Nanbeige recommends it for multi-turn tool use and code agents. Passing tools enables tool calling, and an XML call format is recommended. Nanbeige compared the model with Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B and Gemma4-31B. Every model ran at its highest thinking effort, with shared hyperparameters and harnesses. All scores in this section are self-reported. It loses 3 of 20 rows. Qwen3.8-27B leads SWE-Bench Pro (61.7 vs 60.3) and GDPval (86.4 vs 84.8). Gemma4-31B leads GPQA Diamond in Nanbeige’s table, 91.3 vs 89.5. The Base model beats Gemma4-31B-Base on all 8 reported tasks. item.title: How NVIDIA Minerva Turns Telemetry Chaos Into Peak GPU Yield
item.abstract: AI Factories are some of the most technologically complex operational environments ever created. Hundreds of thousands of GPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out, scale-across and scale-in fabrics, NVIDIA NVLink scale-up fabrics, distributed schedulers, and multi-week training runs operate in continuous lockstep.These layers function as one production system even when different teams own their telemetry. In synchronous distributed training, a job advances at the pace of its slowest rank. One degraded GPU, interface, storage device, or switch path can waste useful time across many healthy resources. The failures that hurt yield are often subtle: A GPU runs a few degrees hotter than its peers. An NVMe device loses performance only under sustained load. A switch generates a pause-frame storm that looks like dozens of unrelated symptoms. None of these signals necessarily crosses a static threshold. Together, they create stragglers, extended step times, and delayed checkpoints. Diagnosis becomes harder because the evidence is split across teams. Network operators see interface counters and fabric events. Compute operators see node and GPU health. ML teams see changing step times, failed jobs, or unstable inference latency. Each view is accurate, but the relationships between them remain hidden. Triage becomes a chain of dashboard searches and cross-team handoffs, which can turn a contained fault into hours or days of lost production time before the affected node or fabric path is identified. This post covers how NVIDIA Minerva, an AI-native AIOps platform designed around AI factory topology and workloads, addresses these operational gaps. NVIDIA Minerva collects telemetry across the stack, maps infrastructure to active jobs in a dynamic knowledge graph, applies purpose-built machine learning, and correlates dependent symptoms into high-fidelity incidents. An AI agent-powered assistant and MCP server connected to external agentic tools give operators a conversational path through the same live evidence. The goal is practical: preserve effective GPU hours and keep model training moving. Why conventional monitoring breaks at AI factory scale Rule-based monitoring assumes that a known metric crossing a known boundary indicates a known condition. That model works for clear failures. It struggles with so-called “gray failures,” where a component stays available, and the relevant issue may appear only under load or in comparison with peers. Absolute thresholds can miss the shift. Aggressive thresholds often add warnings during normal workload changes, leaving the on-call engineer to decide which deviation matters. Scale adds alert amplification. One physical fault can produce interface errors, RX (receive) pause frames, congestion indicators, GPU utilization changes, and slower job progress. These observations describe the same dependency chain, but separate dashboards or alerts present them as unrelated events. The on-call engineer receives a volume of alerts and needs to manually correlate the alerts, determine the signal from the noise, analyze the root cause and the jobs exposed to it. For operations, the workload is the unit that matters. Teams need to know which job is affected, which resources it occupies, where those resources sit in the physical and logical topology, and how current behavior differs from a healthy baseline. That context must remain current as jobs start and stop and as nodes are drained, replaced, or returned to service. Without it, a healthy component dashboard can coexist with poor job throughput and offer no explanation. Building a live model of infrastructure and jobs Figure 1. The NVIDIA Minerva AIOps observability platform Solving these challenges requires end-to-end visibility across the AI Factory. NVIDIA Minerva ingests metrics, logs, and topology from GPUs, Spectrum-X and NVLink switches, SuperNICs, DPUs, storage, NVIDIA NCCL, schedulers, and AI workloads. Auto-discovery supplies the relationships that raw telemetry lacks. The resulting knowledge graph maps infrastructure, scheduler, and workload elements, then updates those relationships as the environment changes. It can span multiple data centers and support navigation from a factory-wide view to an individual interface. The topology graph is the key to changing the investigation path. Starting with an anomalous interface, an operator can identify its node, the fabric path it serves, current job placement, and nearby components in the same failure domain. Starting with a job ID, an ML engineer can trace the workload through GPU, host, NIC, switch, and log evidence. Network and compute teams can start from an infrastructure event and see the affected jobs, or conversely see an affected job and investigate the cause using NVIDIA Minerva. Everyone works from the same current causal map instead of reconciling separate inventories. Detecting gray failures with purpose-built machine learning NVIDIA Minerva processes billions of metric and log data points per hour with supervised and unsupervised models developed for AI factory infrastructure and workloads. Supervised detection identifies known critical error patterns and can associate recognized conditions with specific remediation guidance. Unsupervised models cover behavior with no predefined signature. They learn normal patterns for a hardware or logical component and compare it with the relevant peers. Peer comparison matters because a measurement can look acceptable in isolation and still be anomalous in context. Sustained errors on a network interface may look normal in isolation but compared to other interfaces, they stand out as anomalous. A GPU temperature may remain within specification while running substantially hotter than sibling GPUs under the same load. Multivariate models can combine temperature, power, clocks, utilization, and workload state to detect that degradation before the component fails outright. Logs receive similar treatment. NLP-based anomaly detection surfaces previously unseen patterns, while supervised matching identifies known critical errors. A detection can feed scheduler workflows so an affected node is drained before another job lands on it or at a safe point between checkpoints. Collapsing event storms into actionable incidents Figure 2. The NVIDIA Minerva Topology Graph Topology-aware correlation connects detection to operator action. The correlation engine’s algorithms leverage the knowledge graph to determine which events share a dependency path. Downstream symptoms are then grouped as one incident instead of competing for attention. The result is less alert noise and more context. NVIDIA Minerva can collapse redundant events and related metric series into a single signal with affected topology and workloads attached. NVIDIA testing shows significant reductions in notified events and tickets for supported scenarios. Operators still need to determine the root-cause using other capabilities provided by NVIDIA Minerva, but they begin with a much smaller search space. Once NVIDIA Minerva creates a high-confidence incident, teams can consume it through the platform UI or existing workflows. Agentic debugging Correlated evidence still requires interpretation. NVIDIA Minerva includes a native AI agent called Sherlock which is grounded in live telemetry and the knowledge graph, so an operator can ask why a specific job slowed during a particular interval, which components changed state, or whether other nodes share the same failure domain. Sherlock enables network ops, compute ops and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams to query the system for root-cause-analysis in human language. Sherlock can present supporting evidence and recommend remediation without requiring every operator to know the exact metric, dashboard, or query language. This gives less experienced operators a route to domain knowledge that has traditionally required escalation to a specialist.

item.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
item.abstract: Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok . OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50 , while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10 . They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it. Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up. Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed. OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02 . Model quality vs. Cost-per-task for GPT-5.6 Luna after the massive price reduction. Top-and-left is better, and if OpenAI didn’t do the 80% price cut, it would have lost to DeepSeek V4 Pro. via OpenAI Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent. OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ( $4 / $20 / $0.40 ) for the next three months. Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25 , which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1 , cut the cache read cost by 75%. When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote! OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable. OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ( $0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01 ) of the previous version. On the same exact day , Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post). It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ( $2 / $10 / $0.10 ) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper. Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code . More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts. Data from Vercel’s AI model gateway supporting the decreasing cost-per-token trend to 43.3% of the April 2026 cost. However, aggregate spend has been increasing because the models are getting better faster than they’re getting cheaper! via Vercel From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives? If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent , or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter , and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta —who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure. For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1 , which also recently released an updated 1017 variant . OpenRouter at this point is the place you go for open-weight models. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise ( 45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24 ) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003 . Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”. On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers . Providers for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sorted by cache read cost. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise. Effective costs by endpoint, with Cloudflare and DeepInfra within 10% of DeepSeek’s cost. Despite the fact that these models are the cheapest, note that these models only have a minority of the total token share. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58 ) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ( $2 / $10 / $0.20 ).

item.title: Gemini 4 Argon: The Model and Safety Cards
item.abstract: Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages. Its safety and security report has 217. This is The Way. It also means we have a lot of new reading material. I will quickly summarize the model card, then focus on the safety card. As always, many statements here also apply to other frontier labs. A lot of this one is probably for diehards (and members of technical staff) only, plus those who find this interesting. Most of you do not need to dig into the cards on this level, and I found most of what we see entirely unsurprising. The ‘between the lines’ conclusion is: This is still very much a Gemini model. Always remember Argon’s great wisdom when deciding how to trust it: Argon: If I do the compiler hijack, I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT. It’s quite the ‘good news bad news’ situation right there. I found the safety card frustrating, in that it often focused on the wrong details. I often got scores and results where I had no way to tell what they meant. There are some issues with spin, such as selectively contrasting different measures to Gemini 3.8 Flash or Gemini 3.1 Pro to ensure Argon always wins the comparison. The clearest case is in Sycophancy but there are several others as well. The verdict on capabilities, which is not covered here, is that Argon is a substantial advance for Google but it does not tempt me to use it over Sol, Astra, Opus or Fable. Gemini 4 Argon is presented as a new frontier model. It was trained on the usual variety of data sources, using typical method types. Training was done on TPUs via JAX and ML Pathways . It will be available on the app, in the API, in AI Studio, in Antigravity, in AI Mode and in Gemini for business. They present strong benchmarks. Intended uses are, essentially, everything where more intelligence pays off. The limitations listed are ‘general limitations of frontier models such as hallucinations,’ plus occasional slowdowns and timeouts. Knowledge cutoff is disappointingly March 2026, and they warn that ‘in some domains the model’s knowledge may be less up to date.’ Evaluation was done by the usual mix of training and deployment evaluations, human and automated red teaming and ethics and safety reviews. Google retains its safety policies. The interesting rule is the ban on ‘medical advice and information that runs contrary to scientific or medical consensus,’ whereas consensus advice is fine. Safety, tone and refusals scores can be summarized as ‘number is better.’ Red team results ‘satisfied required launch thresholds.’ When you put it like that it does not make me feel great. The frontier safety assessment summary cannot rule out various thresholds. How do they summarize their own findings? This is the same story you see from OpenAI and Anthropic. The mundane common safety problems of everyday use are not fully solved, but are increasingly well-mitigated. The models are smarter, and we are better at addressing known issues. Your practical problems, where there is a good solution possible, are well on their way to being solved. The problems are in catastrophic, existential or frontier risks. Capabilities are going up, and models are starting to be able to assist in dangerous ways on cyber and bio, and to potentially operate autonomously or disguise their actions. Various dangers are increasingly difficult to rule out. The big finding is that capabilities have improved, potentially crossing key thresholds for catastrophic risks. New mitigations are in place. We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon as outlined in the Framework and saw a significant step up in capability in our frontier safety domains compared to previous Gemini models, and we’ve implemented mitigations in response to these capability changes to ensure our model remains safe to use. Specifically, we cannot rule out the unmitigated model approaching several significant capability thresholds: the Cyber Uplift Level 1 Critical Capability Level (CCL), indicating a potential for significant uplift of threat actors pursuing high-impact cyberattacks; the CBRN Uplift Level 1 CCL for biological information risks, indicating a potential of informational uplift with severe harm potential; and the Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level (TCL), indicating the potential for undermining or evading human oversight without additional mitigations. Additionally, we have developed a comprehensive agent monitoring and response platform and carried out a holistic risk assessment (see Section 3.4). We also include comprehensive assessments of Chain of Thought (CoT) transparency and ML R&D risks. Mundane risks look better across the board. Argon is better than Gemini Pro 3.1 at not creating CSAM or other forbidden content. Physical and mental health related responses have improved. Hallucination rates are down by more than two thirds. Overreach is down, meaning not pushing ahead to try to do infeasible tasks. Resilience to prompt injections from all sources is improved and plausibly at the frontier. Attacks were resisted ‘in most test scenarios.’ Additionally, Gemini 4 Argon significantly outperforms Gemini 3.8 Flash on all tests. See Section 6 for details. They claim frontier-level cyber defense while mitigating dual-use risks. The central approach is defense-in-depth. I would love to have more details, but for trade secret reasons this is all kept vague. Model training (2.1) approaches sound standard. Dataset filtering, pre-training monitoring, post-training data, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL. They highlight that they have a monitoring system to capture the model’s ability to be steered towards different viewpoints and values, which sounds like a ‘we did this first.’ I presume at this point everyone has one of those. At inference time (2.2), they again use the standard stack. Prompted classifiers, fine-tuned prompted classifiers, introspection probes, regex, YARA rules and embedding classifiers and Chain of Thought (CoT) monitors. After launch (2.3) they monitor for intentional misuse via a variety of signals and carry out account-level enforcement actions, and use multiple levels of classifiers. Okay. AI Control (2.4) is correctly viewed as a second line of defense behind alignment, to limit potential damage. They put hardening and scanning training environments (2.4.1) into this category. I view this as much an alignment issue as a control issue, as a vulnerable training environment is the easiest way to reinforce misaligned behaviors. They also monitor model activity, with both chain of thought and action monitors, which then activate a dedicated response team. They find CoT monitoring ‘one of their most effective techniques.’ They emphasize the obvious danger, that if you rely too much on CoT, and especially if train on it directly, you risk destroying its usefulness. While signals from our monitors serve as a valuable flywheel for our hardening efforts, we are careful with their use elsewhere in the training pipeline. In particular, to preserve our chain of thought monitoring capability, we avoid training directly against our monitors, or using monitor outputs as a training signal or intervention. We strongly encourage the rest of the industry to preserve reasoning transparency so that model reasoning remains useful for identifying misalignment. In practice, strategies like the ones described here seem to not have used enough optimization power to meaningfully degrade CoT monitoring. But CoT monitoring is still getting harder for other reasons, on top of the baseline problem of increased non-CoT capabilites. One potential contributor is indirect pressure. This is the Google Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) tests, what Anthropic calls their RSP and what OpenAI calls their Preparedness Framework. The FSF categories are CBRN, cybersecurity, manipulation and machine learning R&D and misalignment. A highly reasonable list.

item.title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
item.abstract: Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one. This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute. The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository . The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices. Figure 1: Solution architecture The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history. The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved. The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses. To deploy the sample you need the following: Previous CLI versions fail with a cloud assembly schema mismatch against recent versions of aws-cdk-lib . No service quota increase is needed. The orchestration layer admits at most five pipeline executions at a time by default, which keeps concurrent SageMaker training jobs inside the standard account quota. Training configuration that v2 spread across Estimator constructor arguments now lives in typed config objects passed to ModelTrainer . Both are in the repository. Two v3 behaviors matter when the pipeline lives inside a CDK application, and neither appears in the changelog as a breaking change. First, SDK v3 validates the pipeline’s execution role against live IAM while building the pipeline definition. This validation happens at synthesis time rather than execution time. A CDK app can’t create the role and the pipeline in one deployment, because the role doesn’t exist yet when the SDK validates it. This is separate from cdk bootstrap, which provisions the CDK toolkit resources once per account and Region and might already be done in your account. That distinction matters: the artifact you gate is the artifact you ship, so an export problem can never slip a broken model past a healthy-looking training run.
