item.title: Building Your First AI Agent in Python with the OpenAI Agents SDK
item.abstract: Building Your First AI Agent in Python with the OpenAI Agents SDK Build your first AI agent in Python with the OpenAI Agents SDK, adding web search, Python tools, conversation memory, and tracing in a simple end-to-end workflow. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 26, 2026 in Python Building an AI agent in Python is now much simpler than it used to be. With the OpenAI Agents SDK , you can create agents, connect tools, maintain conversation state, and run multi-step workflows without building your own tool-calling loop from scratch. In this tutorial, we will build a practical research agent that can search the web, call a custom Python function, remember previous messages, and decide when to use each capability . What Is an AI Agent? A standard large language model (LLM) application usually follows a simple flow: Prompt — Model — Response The model receives a prompt, generates an answer, and stops. An AI agent adds tools and an execution loop : User — Agent — Tool if needed — Agent — Final Response Instead of only generating text, the agent can decide whether it needs to take an action first, such as searching the web, calling a Python function, or retrieving information from memory. With the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Runner manages this process automatically. It sends the request to the model, executes any requested tools, passes the results back to the agent, and continues until the agent produces a final answer. This ability to reason, use tools, and continue working across multiple steps is what makes an agent different from a basic LLM application. Set Up the Project Before we build the agent, let's create a clean Python environment and install everything we need. Create a Python project with uv : mkdir first-ai-agent cd first-ai-agent uv init uv add openai-agents Or install the package with pip : pip install openai-agents Set your OpenAI API key: export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key" On Windows, export works in Git Bash. In Command Prompt or PowerShell, you can use: setx OPENAI_API_KEY "your-api-key" Build Your First Agent Now we can turn a few lines of Python into an agent that decides when it needs fresh information from the web. Create main.py : from agents import Agent, Runner, WebSearchTool agent = Agent( name="Research Assistant", instructions=( "You are a concise research assistant. " "Use web search when current information is required." ), tools=[WebSearchTool()], ) result = Runner.run_sync( agent, "What are the latest developments in Python?" ) print(result.final_output) Run it: uv run main.py Output: As of **September 14, 2026**, the major Python developments are: - **Python 3.14 is the latest stable feature series**; the newest maintenance release is **3.14.7**. It adds officially supported free-threaded builds, deferred annotation evaluation, template string literals (`t""`), ... - **Python 3.15 is nearing release**: the final release is scheduled for **October 1, 2026**. ... For new projects, **Python 3.14.7** is currently the safest default. WebSearchTool() is a hosted OpenAI tool, so the model can decide when it needs current information instead of you manually calling a search API. For example, our run correctly identified Python 3.14.7 as the current stable release. Add Your Own Python Tool Web search is useful, but agents become much more powerful when they can also interact with your own Python code. Add a calculation tool: from agents.decorators import tool @tool def calculate_total( price: float, quantity: int ) -> float: """Calculate the total cost of an order.""" return price * quantity Then give it to the agent: agent = Agent( name="Assistant", instructions="Help with research and calculations.", tools=[ WebSearchTool(), calculate_total, ], ) Test it: result = Runner.run_sync( agent, "I need 14 GPUs costing $2.49 each per hour. " "What will they cost per hour?" ) print(result.final_output) Output: 14 GPUs x $2.49/hour = **$34.86 per hour**. The SDK automatically uses the function name, arguments, type hints, and docstring to create a tool schema the model can understand. You do not need to manually define JSON schemas or write the tool-calling loop yourself. Tip: Write clear docstrings because they help the model understand what a tool does and when it should use it. Adding Conversation Memory A useful agent should not forget everything the moment the next message arrives, so let's give it conversation memory. To make the agent conversational, add a session: from agents import SQLiteSession session = SQLiteSession( "user_1", "conversations.db" ) Then pass it into each run: while True: message = input("You: ") if message.lower() in {"exit", "quit"}: break result = Runner.run_sync( agent, message, session=session, ) print("Agent:", result.final_output) Now try: The second request automatically receives the earlier conversation, so the agent understands what "the latest version" refers to. Because we used a file-backed SQLite database, the history can also persist after restarting the program. For larger applications, the SDK also provides session backends for systems such as Redis, SQLAlchemy, and MongoDB . How the Complete Agent Works At this point, all the pieces come together: The agent decides what action to take , the Runner executes the agent loop and any requested tools , and the session preserves conversation history between requests. Here is the complete main.py : import os import sys from agents import Agent, Runner, SQLiteSession, WebSearchTool from agents.decorators import tool @tool def calculate_total( price: float, quantity: int ) -> float: """Calculate the total cost of an order.""" return price * quantity def main() -> None: if not os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY"): sys.exit( "Error: set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable first." ) agent = Agent( name="Assistant", instructions=""" Help the user with research and calculations. Use the available tools when necessary. """, tools=[ WebSearchTool(), calculate_total, ], ) session = SQLiteSession( "user_1", "conversations.db" ) try: while True: try: message = input("You: ") except (EOFError, KeyboardInterrupt): print() break command = message.strip().lower() if command in {"exit", "quit"}: break if not command: continue try: result = Runner.run_sync( agent, message, session=session, ) except Exception as exc: print( f"Agent error " f"({type(exc).__name__}): {exc}" ) continue print("Agent:", result.final_output) finally: session.close() if __name__ == "__main__": main() This gives us a small but complete conversational agent with web search, a custom Python tool, persistent memory, basic error handling, and a continuous chat interface . The Agents SDK also enables tracing by default , which is especially useful once your workflows become more complex. Traces let you inspect the model calls, tool usage, handoffs, and other steps taken during an agent run. You can inspect these traces in the OpenAI dashboard to understand how the agent reached its answer, which tools it selected, and where problems occurred. This makes tracing particularly useful for debugging tool-calling behavior and improving agent instructions. Final Thoughts Building your first AI agent is less about creating a complex autonomous system and more about giving a model the ability to take useful actions . In this guide, we started with a simple agent, added web search , connected a custom Python tool , introduced persistent conversation memory , and brought everything together in a complete application with tracing and error handling. That foundation is enough to build surprisingly capable workflows. From here, you can gradually add APIs, MCP servers, guardrails, handoffs, more specialized tools, and additional agents as your application grows. The pattern stays the same: give the agent the right tools, let it decide when to use them, and let the Agents SDK handle the execution loop .

item.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
item.abstract: News AI Business The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.﻿ Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.﻿ by Mia Sato Oct 26, 2026, 5:30 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools. The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer. After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge ’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves. Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days. But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites. An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up. item.title: Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis?
item.abstract: AI Report Tech Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis? The ancient code holding the world together may meet its match in AI. Today is not that day. by Robert Hart Oct 26, 2026, 1:15 PM UTC A computer running COBOL 73, an antiquated computer programming language, awaits taxpayer information entries at the Internal Revenue Service in Austin, Tx., on Friday, June 10, 2022. | Image: Getty Images Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . What do the IRS, banks, airlines, and government infrastructure around the world have in common? They’re all running on systems propped up by antique computer code that nobody dares touch, lest everything come crashing down. OpenAI thinks it may have a solution. On October 19th, the company touted “substantial improvements” in its latest AI models’ ability to migrate aging software written in older programming languages into modern code, which it claims could help organizations with “maintaining and modernizing older systems.” That’s a potentially massive deal. COBOL, one of the languages highlighted by OpenAI, remains stubbornly embedded in vast portions of the world’s critical infrastructure. And despite decades of efforts to banish it to history, the language has limped on, simply refusing to die. “Nobody in their right mind would use COBOL for a new development project.” It is hard to overstate COBOL’s ubiquity. Short for “common business-oriented language,” COBOL came into being in 1959. Nearly seven decades later, it is still everywhere. According to IBM , COBOL is the foundation for more than 40 percent of online banking systems, supports 80 percent of in-person credit card transactions, and handles 95 percent of ATM transactions. It also underpins many government systems, from Social Security to the IRS to services run by most states . One rough estimate puts the annual cost of COBOL’s inefficiencies to the US GDP at around $105 billion. But replacing COBOL is fiendishly difficult. The same goes for other legacy programming languages, like Fortran, still in use today for everything from scientific computing and weather forecasting to atmospheric and ocean studies and codes critical to nuclear security . These systems are often too important to risk breaking, and many of the programmers who understand them have long since retired or died. For all their impressive advances in modern software development , AI coding tools have struggled to make much headway with these legacy systems. But recent developments suggest that may be changing. In its latest blog post, OpenAI reported promising results migrating COBOL code to more modern programming languages, including C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust, without changing what the original software does. That last bit is crucial for organizations looking to ditch code like COBOL, and OpenAI acknowledges that “a migration is considered successful only if all tests pass.” In OpenAI’s own tests, GPT-6.1 Sol achieved 87 percent behavior preservation accuracy at low reasoning effort — how many computational steps the model spends analyzing a problem before giving an answer — climbing to 98 percent at higher reasoning. By comparison, at low reasoning effort, GPT-6 Astra scored around 86 percent, GPT-6 Sol just 21 percent, and GPT-5.6 Sol a mere 5 percent. “Rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system.” “These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on,” OpenAI wrote. The company also reported improvements on its models’ ability to build database software in various programming languages, including COBOL. Anthropic also sees an opportunity in legacy systems. In February, it published a step-by-step “code modernization playbook” and pitched its coding agent, Claude Code, as a way to migrate COBOL code into modern languages like Java or Python. It offered no performance benchmarks showing how well Claude Code could perform such migrations, but declared that “the economics of COBOL modernization have shifted.” Shares in IBM, which derives part of its revenue helping companies maintain legacy systems, nosedived following Anthropic’s announcement. Experts who spoke to The Verge agreed that AI tools have made strides in tackling legacy code in recent years. But they cautioned that advances trumpeted by OpenAI this week are a very long way from making it possible to safely replace critical legacy systems built around it. OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines acknowledged in an email to The Verge that legacy code “is still far from a solved problem” and said the company is listening to feedback from developers and enterprises and exploring ways to build better tests and continue improving its models’ understanding of coding languages. Anthropic did not provide comment in time for publication. “The evaluations shown by OpenAI don’t address the key difficulty: Breaking up a complex legacy system into smaller units that can be replaced individually.” “Rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system,” said Vadim Zaytsev, an associate professor of software evolution at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. Systems do have a lot of code — Zaytsev said the largest system he’d seen had 250 million lines of COBOL, “definitely not the world’s largest” — but that’s only part of the problem. Code may be written in multiple languages and there’s data, potentially stored in various formats, to consider, he said. There are also technical integrations with other systems and the expectations of the people and organizations to bear in mind. All that complexity means “AI is not playing a major role at the moment in replacing or migrating legacy COBOL systems,” Zaytsev said. OpenAI’s evaluations don’t capture this complex reality either, Arie van Deursen, a software engineering professor at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, told The Verge . He described the company’s blog as “superficial,” noting it offered few details about the migration task, while its language benchmark tested models on a relatively simple and well-defined task involving systems similar to those they would have encountered in training. He also stressed the huge gap between maintaining an aging system and modernizing it. “Maintaining is of course a lot easier than modernizing,” van Deursen said, calling the tasks OpenAI used to assess its models “lightyears” away from actual modernization. “The evaluations shown by OpenAI don’t address the key difficulty: Breaking up a complex legacy system into smaller units that can be replaced individually.” The biggest challenge isn’t necessarily rewriting code. “The main challenge is indeed not understanding how the system works,” said Alastair Donaldson, a professor of programming languages at Imperial College London. Such a lack of understanding is a “very common” problem for legacy systems using languages like COBOL, he said, adding that very few people know how to program in them anymore. And while it is everywhere, Donaldson said “nobody in their right mind would use COBOL for a new development project.” “In many cases even minor differences in system behaviour before and after migration are unacceptable.” That makes robust testing crucial, Donaldson said. One approach could be to run the same workflows through the old and new systems to check they behave identically. AI could also document its code translation, ideally allowing humans familiar with the legacy language to review the work. Formal verification, which uses mathematical techniques to computationally verify that code behaves correctly, is another option, said Jacopo Mauro, a mathematics and computer science professor at the University of Southern Denmark.
